recipe.history:
The smash burger is, at its core, an American invention born of pragmatism and the physics of a flat-top griddle. Its conceptual origins stretch back to the early twentieth century, when roadside stands and lunch counters began cooking thin, crispy-edged beef patties on cast-iron or steel surfaces heated by gas flames or wood-fired coals. The technique — pressing a ball of ground beef hard against a searing-hot flat surface — maximizes the contact area between beef and metal, triggering the Maillard reaction across the widest possible cross-section of the patty in the shortest possible time. The result is a burger with an almost lacquer-like crust of caramelized beef proteins and rendered fat, paper-thin crispy edges, and a center that remains moist and yielding. The smash burger as a formal category entered the popular American consciousness most visibly through regional chains like Steak 'n Shake (founded 1934 in Normal, Illinois) and later through the eponymous Smashburger chain and the NYC-born J.G. Melon tradition — but long before branding entered the equation, short-order cooks across the country had been smashing balls of beef instinctively, understanding in their hands what food science would later confirm in laboratories. The electric griddle, introduced widely into American home and commercial kitchens in the postwar era, proved to be an exceptional surface for this technique — its even, consistent heat delivering a more uniform crust than the variable hotspots of a gas flame.

American cheese — the other essential protagonist of this burger — has a history as interesting and underappreciated as the smash technique itself. Developed in the early twentieth century by James L. Kraft, who patented a process for pasteurizing and emulsifying natural cheese into a shelf-stable product in 1916, American cheese was initially a practical solution to wartime food distribution needs. The U.S. military adopted it en masse during both World Wars for its shelf stability and caloric density. After the war, it entered the civilian kitchen and never left. Its defining characteristic — the addition of emulsifying salts, specifically sodium citrate — gives it a melting behavior unmatched by any natural cheese: it flows, clings, and coats in a smooth, glossy sheet, bonding to the surface of a hot beef patty in a way that aged cheddar or Gruyère simply cannot replicate. On a smash burger, American cheese is not a compromise. It is the correct tool for the job, engineered by accident of history to perform exactly this function.

I came to appreciate the electric griddle as a serious cooking instrument reluctantly. I was a gas-stove devotee for years, convinced that the instant responsiveness of an open flame was indispensable to real cooking. The first time I tried making smash burgers on a borrowed electric griddle at a friend's backyard cookout, I expected disappointment. What I got instead was the single most evenly crusted smash burger I had ever produced — the griddle's flat, consistent surface delivering heat with a democracy that a gas burner's uneven flame simply couldn't match. The edges of each patty came out in a perfect jagged lacework of crisp, dark beef, the cheese melted in a glassy sheet, and the special sauce I had mixed in a bowl on the side married everything into something that tasted like a distillation of every great diner burger I had ever eaten. I have never been smug about cooking fuel since. The tool matters less than the technique, and the technique here is everything.

Cooking a smash burger patty to medium rare requires more precision than people assume. Because the patties are thin — typically two to three ounces smashed to roughly a quarter inch — the window between medium rare and overcooked is measured in seconds, not minutes. The target is 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) at the center, achieved quickly over very high heat so the exterior maximally browns without the interior overcooking. A double-smash formation — two thin patties per burger — allows you to stack cheese between the layers and hit that temperature window with better control than a single thick patty. At medium rare, even these thin patties retain a faint blush and carry the rendered fat that makes each bite unctuous and satisfying. Well-done smash burgers are an exercise in chewing dry protein, and they represent a failure of both nerve and thermometer.
ingredients: 2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour, plus more for dusting
2 large eggs (1 whole egg for dough, 1 beaten for egg wash)
4 tbsp unsalted butter, softened and cubed
For the smash burger patties (makes 4 double-smash burgers, 8 patties total):
1 small white onion, very finely minced
Neutral oil (such as canola or vegetable), for the griddle
instructions: 1. Make the brioche buns: In the bowl of a stand mixer, combine the warm water, 1 tablespoon of the sugar, and the yeast. Let bloom 5 minutes until foamy. Add the flour, remaining 2 tablespoons sugar, salt, 1 whole egg, and warm milk. Mix on low with the dough hook until a shaggy dough forms, about 2 minutes. Increase to medium and add the softened butter one cube at a time, waiting until each piece is incorporated before adding the next. Continue kneading 8 to 10 minutes until the dough is smooth, glossy, and pulls cleanly from the bowl sides.

2. Transfer the dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise at room temperature 1 to 1 1/2 hours until doubled. Punch down, divide into 4 equal portions (roughly 120g each), and shape into tight smooth balls. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover with a damp towel, and proof 45 minutes until puffed.

3. Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush each bun with beaten egg and sprinkle generously with sesame seeds. Bake 15 to 18 minutes until deep golden brown. Cool on a wire rack at least 20 minutes before slicing.

4. Make the special sauce: Whisk together the mayonnaise, ketchup, sweet pickle relish, yellow mustard, white wine vinegar, garlic powder, onion powder, smoked paprika, and salt in a bowl until fully combined. Taste and adjust salt or vinegar. Cover and refrigerate at least 30 minutes for the flavors to meld.

5. Divide the ground beef into 8 equal portions (4 oz / 113g each). Roll each loosely into a ball — do not pack tightly. Season each ball with a pinch of salt and pepper on the outside just before cooking. Do not form flat patties yet; the smashing happens on the griddle.

6. Place an electric griddle (or large flat cast-iron griddle) over its highest heat setting, or on your stove's largest burner set to high. Lightly coat the surface with neutral oil using a folded paper towel or brush. Heat until the surface is shimmering and a drop of water evaporates instantly on contact.

7. Working in batches of 2 to 4 depending on griddle size, place a beef ball on the griddle. Immediately place a square of parchment paper over the ball and, using a sturdy flat spatula or burger press, smash the ball firmly and decisively into a patty approximately 1/4 inch thick and 4 to 5 inches across. Apply maximum downward pressure for 10 full seconds. Remove the parchment. Repeat for remaining balls.

8. Cook the smashed patties without moving them for 90 seconds to 2 minutes until the edges are deeply brown, lacy, and crisp and the top surface is beginning to turn gray-brown. Season the cooked side with additional salt and pepper.

9. Flip each patty with a thin metal spatula, scraping up the full crust from the griddle surface. Immediately place one slice of American cheese on each patty. After flipping, immediately top 4 of the patties with the minced white onion (approximately 1 teaspoon per patty). Stack a second cheese-topped patty directly on top of each onion-covered patty to form a double-smash stack.

10. Check the internal temperature of each double-smash stack — the target is 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C). If needed, cover loosely with a metal dome for 30 to 60 additional seconds to melt the cheese and bring the interior up to temperature. Remove from the griddle and rest 2 minutes.
11. While the patties rest, split the brioche buns and toast them cut-side down on the hot griddle for 60 to 90 seconds until lightly golden and crisped.

12. Assemble: Spread a generous tablespoon of special sauce on both the top and bottom bun halves. On the bottom bun, layer the shredded iceberg lettuce, then 2 tomato slices, then the pickle chips. Place the double-smash stack on top. Cap with the top bun and press gently. Serve immediately.
